summary: This informational memo from Cisco gives an overview of tag switching, a way of forwarding packets by looking up a short label instead of the full destination address. It describes the two main parts, forwarding and control. It is a vendor description, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Tag switching is a way for routers to forward packets. Each packet carries a short label, and the router looks the label up in a table to find out where to send the packet next. The rules for handing out those labels sit apart from the rule for forwarding, so the forwarding can stay fast and simple while the routing behind it changes.

subtitle: A router design that forwards packets by swapping a short tag instead of looking up the destination address.

tldr.problem: Routers have to look up a destination address on every packet, and that lookup gets slower as the routing table grows and as more traffic has to be handled.
tldr.mechanism: Tag switching gives each packet a short tag. A switch looks the tag up in a table, replaces it with the outgoing tag, and sends the packet, while the routing protocols that already exist work out which tags mean what.
tldr.outcome: The forwarding step becomes a fixed-length lookup that can be built into hardware, and the control part stays separate from it, so new routing functions can be added without changing how packets are forwarded.

today: RFC 2105 is an Informational memo from February 1997, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The IESG note in the document itself records that the protocol was not the product of an IETF working group and was not on the standards track, and its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.

sections.title: Introduction and the Two Components
sections.content:
Continuous growth of the Internet demands higher bandwidth within the Internet service providers, and demand for higher bandwidth also comes from emerging multimedia applications. Higher bandwidth in turn requires higher forwarding performance, measured in packets per second, by routers, for both multicast and unicast traffic. Growth also demands improved scaling properties of the Internet routing system: the ability to contain the volume of routing information maintained by individual routers, and the ability to build a hierarchy of routing knowledge.

Tag switching is offered as a technology that provides an efficient solution to these challenges. It blends the flexibility and rich functionality of network layer routing with the simplicity of the label swapping forwarding paradigm. The simplicity of label swapping enables improved forwarding performance while maintaining competitive price and performance, and by associating a wide range of forwarding granularities with a tag, the same forwarding paradigm can support destination-based routing, multicast, a hierarchy of routing knowledge and flexible routing control. A combination of simple forwarding, a wide range of forwarding granularities and the ability to evolve routing functionality while preserving the same forwarding paradigm is what enables a routing system to evolve gracefully.

Tag switching consists of two components. The forwarding component uses the tag information carried by packets, and the tag forwarding information maintained by a tag switch, to perform packet forwarding. The control component is responsible for maintaining correct tag forwarding information among a group of interconnected tag switches. An IESG note records that this protocol is not the product of an IETF working group and is not a standards track document, and that it has not necessarily benefited from the widespread and in depth community review that standards track documents receive.
sections.plainLanguage: The split between forwarding and control is the central idea. Forwarding is the quick per-packet decision; control is the slower work of deciding what the forwarding table should say.

sections.title: Forwarding by Label Swapping
sections.content:
The fundamental forwarding paradigm is based on label swapping. When a packet with a tag arrives at a tag switch, the switch uses the tag as an index in its Tag Information Base (TIB). Each entry in the TIB consists of an incoming tag and one or more sub-entries of the form outgoing tag, outgoing interface and outgoing link level information. If the switch finds an entry whose incoming tag equals the tag in the packet, then for each such sub-entry the switch replaces the tag in the packet with the outgoing tag, replaces the link level information in the packet with the outgoing link level information, and forwards the packet over the outgoing interface.

Two observations follow. First, the forwarding decision is based on an exact match using a fixed length, fairly short tag as an index, rather than the longest match forwarding traditionally used at the network layer. That simplifies the forwarding procedure and enables higher forwarding performance, and the procedure is simple enough for a straightforward hardware implementation. Second, the forwarding decision is independent of the tag's forwarding granularity: the same algorithm applies to unicast and to multicast, a unicast entry simply having a single sub-entry while a multicast entry may have one or more.

The tag can be carried in a packet in several ways: as a small shim tag header inserted between the layer 2 and the network layer headers; as part of the layer 2 header, if that header provides adequate semantics, as with ATM; or as part of the network layer header, for example using the Flow Label field in IPv6 with appropriately modified semantics. So tag switching can be implemented over virtually any media type, including point-to-point links, multi-access links and ATM. The forwarding component is also network layer independent, so using a control component specific to a particular network layer protocol lets tag switching work with different network layer protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: One table lookup replaces the address lookup, and the lookup is on a fixed-length value rather than a prefix, so the hardware can do it the same way every time.

sections.title: The Control Component and Tag Allocation
sections.content:
Essential to tag switching is the binding between a tag and network layer routing. To provide good scaling characteristics while accommodating diverse routing functionality, tag switching supports a wide range of forwarding granularities: at one extreme a tag could be bound to a group of routes, more specifically to the network layer reachability information of the routes in the group, and at the other extreme a tag could be bound to an individual application flow such as an RSVP flow. A tag could also be bound to a multicast tree. The control component creates those bindings and then distributes the binding information among the tag switches, and it is organized as a collection of modules, each supporting a particular routing function, so that new modules can be added.

For destination-based routing, a tag switch participates in routing protocols such as OSPF and BGP and builds its FIB from what those protocols tell it. There are three permitted methods for tag allocation and TIB management: downstream tag allocation, downstream tag allocation on demand, and upstream tag allocation. In all cases a switch allocates tags and binds them to address prefixes in its FIB. In downstream allocation the tag carried in a packet is generated and bound to a prefix by the switch at the downstream end of the link, with respect to the direction of data flow; in upstream allocation the tags are allocated and bound at the upstream end of the link. On demand allocation means that tags are only allocated and distributed by the downstream switch when the upstream switch asks for it. The memo notes that the on demand and upstream methods are most useful in ATM networks.

Under downstream allocation, for each route in its FIB the switch allocates a tag, creates a TIB entry with the incoming tag set to that tag, and advertises the binding between the incoming tag and the route to adjacent tag switches, either by piggybacking the binding on the existing routing protocols or by using a separate Tag Distribution Protocol (TDP). When a switch receives tag binding information for a route that was originated by the next hop for that route, it puts the tag into the outgoing tag of the TIB entry, creating the binding between the outgoing tag and the route. Under on demand allocation the switch identifies the next hop for each route and requests a binding for it, and the next hop allocates a tag, creates its own TIB entry and returns the binding. Under upstream allocation a switch with point-to-point interfaces allocates a tag for each route reachable over such an interface, creates a TIB entry with the outgoing tag set to it, and advertises the binding to the next hop, which places the tag into the incoming tag of its own entry.

Once a TIB entry has both an incoming and an outgoing tag, the switch can forward packets for the bound routes using the forwarding algorithm. When a switch creates a binding it also updates its FIB, which lets it add tags to previously untagged packets. The scaling comes from the fact that the total number of tags a switch must maintain cannot be greater than the number of routes in its FIB, and in some cases a single tag can be associated with a group of routes. Tag allocation is driven by topology rather than traffic: it is the existence of a FIB entry that causes an allocation, not the arrival of data packets. Using tags for routes rather than flows also removes the need to classify every flow, which makes the scheme more robust and stable when traffic patterns change.
sections.plainLanguage: The routing protocols stay as they are, and a separate mechanism says which tag stands for which route. Who picks the tag is a choice: the far end of the link, the far end when asked, or the near end.

sections.title: Hierarchy of Routing Knowledge
sections.content:
The IP routing architecture models a network as a collection of routing domains. Within a domain, routing is provided by interior routing such as OSPF, and across domains by exterior routing such as BGP. All routers within domains that carry transit traffic have to maintain information from exterior routing as well as interior routing, and that is a problem: the amount of information is not insignificant, it places additional demand on router resources, and an increase in routing information quite often increases convergence time, which degrades the overall performance of the system.

Tag switching allows the decoupling of interior and exterior routing, so that only tag switches at the border of a domain maintain the information provided by exterior routing, while all other switches in the domain maintain only what the domain's interior routing provides, which is usually significantly smaller. This reduces the routing load on non-border switches and shortens convergence time.

To support this, tag switching allows a packet to carry not one but a set of tags, organized as a stack. A tag switch can swap the tag at the top of the stack, pop the stack, or swap the tag and push one or more tags onto the stack. When a packet is forwarded between two border tag switches in different domains the stack contains just one tag; when it is forwarded within a domain the stack contains two, the second pushed by the domain's ingress border switch. The tag at the top provides forwarding to the appropriate egress border switch, and the next tag provides correct forwarding at the egress switch. The stack is popped by either the egress switch or the penultimate switch. The control component here is similar to the one used with destination-based routing; the only essential difference is that the tag binding information is distributed both among physically adjacent tag switches and among border tag switches within a domain, and the memo notes that the latter could be accommodated by minor extensions to BGP through a separate tag binding attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside a network, a router only needs to know about that network. The outside world is handled at the edges, which keeps the tables small and the network quick to settle after a change.

sections.title: Multicast and Flexible Routing
sections.content:
Essential to multicast routing is the notion of spanning trees. Multicast routing procedures such as PIM construct those trees with receivers as leaves, and multicast forwarding forwards the packets along them. To support multicast forwarding with tag switching, a tag switch associates a tag with a multicast tree. When the switch creates a multicast forwarding entry, for a shared tree or a source-specific tree, and the list of outgoing interfaces for the entry, it also creates local tags, one per outgoing interface. It creates an entry in its TIB and populates the outgoing tag, outgoing interface and outgoing MAC header for each outgoing interface, placing a locally generated tag in the outgoing tag field. That creates a binding between the multicast tree and the tags, and the switch then advertises, over each outgoing interface, the binding between the tag associated with that interface and the tree. When a switch receives a binding between a multicast tree and a tag from another switch, and that other switch is the upstream neighbour with respect to the tree, the local switch puts the tag into the incoming tag component of the TIB entry. When switches are interconnected via a multiple-access subnetwork, the tag allocation procedure for multicast has to be coordinated among them.

Flexible routing, or explicit routes, addresses a limitation of destination-based routing. The only information from a packet used to forward it is the destination address, which enables highly scalable routing but limits the ability to influence the actual paths packets take. That in turn limits the ability to even out traffic across multiple links, to take load off heavily used links and shift it towards less used ones, and, for providers who support different classes of service, to segregate those classes by the links they use. Some providers use Frame Relay or ATM to overcome these limits; tag switching, because of the flexible granularity of tags, can overcome them without either. To provide forwarding along paths different from the ones determined by destination-based routing, the control component allows tag bindings to be installed in tag switches that do not correspond to the destination-based routing paths.
sections.plainLanguage: Because a tag can mean different things, the same forwarding machinery can carry a multicast tree or a chosen path across the network, not just a destination address.

sections.title: ATM, Quality of Service and Deployment
sections.content:
Because the tag switching forwarding paradigm is based on label swapping, and ATM forwarding is also based on label swapping, tag switching can readily be applied to ATM switches by implementing the control component. The tag information can be carried in the VCI field; if two levels of tagging are needed the VPI field could be used as well, although the size of the VPI field limits the size of the networks in which that would be practical. To obtain the necessary control information the switch should be able, at a minimum, to participate as a peer in network layer routing protocols such as OSPF and BGP, and if the switch has to perform routing information aggregation it should also be able to perform network layer forwarding for some fraction of the traffic.

Supporting destination-based routing with tag switching on an ATM switch may require the switch to maintain not one but several tags associated with a route or a group of routes with the same next hop, to avoid interleaving packets that arrive from different upstream tag switches but are sent concurrently to the same next hop. Either the on demand or the upstream allocation scheme could be used. Implementing tag switching on an ATM switch would simplify integration between ATM switches and routers, since an ATM switch capable of tag switching would appear as a router to an adjacent router, and it removes the need for ATM addressing, routing and signalling schemes. It does not preclude supporting a traditional ATM control plane such as PNNI on the same switch, with the two components operating in what the memo calls a Ships In the Night mode, with the VPI and VCI space and other resources partitioned so the components do not interact.

For quality of service, two mechanisms are needed: classifying packets into classes, and ensuring that the handling of packets gives each class the right characteristics such as bandwidth and loss. Tag switching gives an easy way to mark packets as belonging to a class once they have been classified the first time. Initial classification uses information carried in the network layer or higher layer headers, and a tag corresponding to the resulting class is applied to the packet. Tagged packets can then be handled efficiently by the tag switching routers along their path without being reclassified. If RSVP is used to request a quality of service for a class of packets, a tag must be allocated for each RSVP session for which state is installed at a tag switch, which might be done by TDP or by an extension of RSVP.

For deployment, tag switching is performed between a pair of adjacent tag switches and the binding information could be distributed on a pairwise basis, so it can be introduced in a simple, incremental fashion. Once a pair of adjacent routers are converted into tag switches, each tags packets destined for the other. Because tag switches use the same routing protocols as routers, their introduction has no impact on routers, and a tag switch connected to a router acts just as a router from the router's point of view. As more routers are upgraded, the scope of functionality widens: once all the routers within a domain support tag switching, the hierarchy of routing knowledge function can be used. The memo's summary is that tag switching is not constrained to a particular network layer protocol, that its forwarding component is simple enough to allow high performance forwarding, and that its control component is flexible enough to support destination-based routing, multicast routing, a hierarchy of routing knowledge and explicitly defined routes.
sections.plainLanguage: Because ATM switches already swap labels, the same idea fits onto them. And because the two halves are separate, a network can be converted one router at a time without disturbing the routers that have not been converted.
